utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We're now back in open session. We will take a break for half an hour and then we'll hear the next witness, Ms. Mihajlovic. We will resume at 10 past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Will the witness take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Mihajlovic. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Ms. Mihajlovic, as we discussed -- oh, can you please state your name for the record, your full name.

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: My full name is Mira Mihajlovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: As we discussed, part of your evidence in this case will be submitted in writing, and I need to deal first with the formalities associated with that submission. You provided a statement to representatives of the Republika Srpska MUP and were spoken to by representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor in 2005 and on two occasions in 2009; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Have you recently had the opportunity to review with the assistants of an interpreter an amalgamated statement containing relevant excerpts of these interviews?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You provided some clarifications and observations which were incorporated into the signed version of that statement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could I have 65 ter 90313, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Ms. Mihajlovic, on the screen in front of you do you see a statement there, and is that your signature at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you agree that the -- the contents of the signed statement is accurate?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If you were asked today about the same matters that are contained in that statement, would you provide the same information to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender 65 ter 90313, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4358, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And with Your Honours' leave, I'll now read the summary of the witness's written evidence. The witness Mira Mihajlovic was Radovan Karadzic's secretary from the 5th of January, 1993, until the 27th of January, 1996. She worked together with another secretary, Milijana Rasevic, in the presidential office. The witness identifies her handwriting and that of her colleague Rasevic in a log-book maintained by them and in Karadzic's appointment books for 1994 and 1995. The witness explained that the appointment books were maintained to ensure that there was an accurate record of Karadzic's meetings and telephone conversations. A minus symbol would be entered when an appointment or telephone call was scheduled, and this would be converted to a plus symbol once the appointment or telephone call had been completed or realised. The witness explains the process of sending and receiving communications from the president's office to the Republika Srpska Ministry of the Interior, the Army of the Republika Srpska, and other organs. Mrs. Mihajlovic or Ms. Rasevic would generally type up all kinds of presidential documents for Mr. Karadzic. A courier would then deliver the typed document to the republic communications centre where the documents would be encrypted and transmitted to the recipients. Similarly, couriers would deliver incoming messages to the presidential office from the communications centre. With Ms. Rasevic, the witness maintained archives of the presidential documents and records in a filing cabinet in the office. The witness explains how the OBL secured the office and that a security guard was present 24 hours a day. Once Mr. Karadzic had returned home for the evening, a security duty officer was always present in the office to answer the telephone. The witness recalls that Mr. Karadzic conducted all of his meetings behind closed doors, and she would not be present during these meetings and was not asked to make notes of the meetings. That completes the summary of the witness's written evidence, Your Honour. I have a number of questions for Mrs. Mihajlovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mrs. Mihajlovic, in your statement, you state that you and Milijana Rasevic worked every other day and that in your statement you also speak of an internal communication system in relation to Mr. Karadzic's appointment books, and I have just read out the plus sign and the minus sign. You also state, and this is in paragraph 33 of the amalgamated statement, that you would also record the approximate length of the meeting and the call -- or the call and that was usually done in parentheses and at the end of the day you would put a time when you left the office. I would now like to show you a couple of documents, three documents, so that you can show the Trial Chamber how the system actually worked.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have now 65 ter 09178, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told that it hasn't been released yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I apologise for that, Your Honour. Just one moment. It should be available in e-court now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mrs. Mihajlovic, we can see the document on the screen is an interview of "El Pais" journalist Angel Santa Cruz Molina with Radovan Karadzic on the 13th of July, 1995. This is the transcript of the interview. Is this interview consistent with any entries in the appointment book for 1995? And to assist you, is it possible to have on the same screen, the other side of the screen, the right-hand side 65 ter 04754, which is P02242. And if we could go to page 78 of the English and page 90 of the B/C/S. It is for the date the 13th of July, 1995, and I apologise if -- if -- page 90 should -- should be that date. So we need to go forward quite some pages. And the following page, please. Mrs. Mihajlovic, do you see any entries which are consistent with the interview which occurred on the 13th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I do. This interview had been planned, that is obvious, and it was actually held on at that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And is that the last entry that we see for the date of the 13th of July, 1995, in the appointment book on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just to be sure, can we see the English translation of this diary or appointment book.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, it should be on page 78 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What time-frame does it refer to?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The 13th of July, 1995. So we can see on the left-hand side of the screen starting the 13th of July. If we could go to the following page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, you say that the interview happened, and is that because you can see that there's a plus sign before the -- the interview?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did we find the item in the appointment book? What time was it planned at?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mrs. Mihajlovic, if you can tell the Trial Chamber what is in relation to the entry for the interview, what is in brackets, in parentheses, at the end of that entry.

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: The parentheses show the time when the interview commenced and ended. In other words, it commented at 2135 hours, and went on until 2210 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And then on the right-hand side of the notebook, we see the 22.15, and can you explain what that means to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: That means that the president left the office at that time, and that the work-day ended at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender 65 ter 09178, which is the interview with the Spanish journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Object. Object. Objection, Mr. President. I don't believe that this is an accurate foundation for the content of the interview. Simply showing that an interview took place at a certain time doesn't provide evidence of the accuracy of its contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to respond, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I submit that it is relevant and probative and it is linked to this witness's evidence. It may be used to assist the Chamber in assessing the probative value or the weight to be given to the witness's evidence in relation to the system used in the appointment book [overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Can you -- can you upload -- in the meantime, can you upload that interview 9178, at least in English? Yes, please continue, Ms. Sutherland. I'm sorry to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document will assist the Chamber in assessing the probative value or the weight to be given to the witness's evidence in relation to the system used in maintaining the appointment books to verify that a meeting or a telephone call was schedule and whether in fact it actually took place. You have the discretion to admit the document now for this limited reference purpose. And as I said a moment ago, I would submit that it corroborates this witness's evidence as to how the appointment books worked.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, you said that -- what would be your observation with respect to Ms. Sutherland's suggestion, admitting this for limited purpose?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If that were the only purpose for its admission and the contents of the interview would not be taken into account by the Chamber I don't see any problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do have the audio of the ... Your Honour, we do have the audio of that interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But your purpose of tendering this document was to corroborate Ms. Mihajlovic's evidence as to how she recorded all the appointment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we will admit this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's the basis I seek to be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the limited purpose, i.e., not for the content of its truth. We'll give the number for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4359, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have the next document, 65 ter 13763.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mrs. Mihajlovic, this is a summary of an interview of Dr. Radovan Karadzic with the Bosnian Serb television on the 4th of August, 1995. Is this interview consistent with any entries in the appointment book? And in order to assist, if we could have again Exhibit P02242 on the screen, and if we could go to page 102 in the B/C/S. And page 88 in the English. Mrs. Mihajlovic, do you see there in the B/C/S on the right-hand side of the screen any entry there which is consistent with the interview of Dr. Karadzic with the Bosnian Serb television on the 4th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This -- this was the last entry for that day at 2100 hours, "guest appearance on TV."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the entry has a plus sign next to it.

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Which means according to your earlier testimony that that actually occurred; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And then we see the -- on the right-hand side of the page 0015 hours.

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And again, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: That means that our work-day ended at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, if we could have the document back on the screen, 13763, please. Your Honour, I seek to tender that document, again for the limited purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit it for limited purpose, i.e., for the purpose of corroborating Ms. Mihajlovic's evidence as to the method of keeping -- or, Mr. Karadzic's appointment book, and we'll give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 4360, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the final document is 65 ter 13684.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mrs. Mihajlovic, as you can see, this is a 1st Krajina Corps report dated the 30th of September, 1995, regarding a meeting of Republika Srpska government with municipal War Presidency representatives on the 29th of September, 1995, which was chaired by the president and the prime minister and one other. Is this report of a meeting that stated that the president participated consistent with any entries in the appointment book?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And again if we could assist the witness with Exhibit P02242, the 1995 appointment book, and if we could go to B/C/S page 116. And the English, page 96. So we can -- I think it may be page 119 in the B/C/S. I'm sorry. We can see in the English down the bottom it starts the 29th of September, 1995. And in the B/C/S, could we go back one more page, and one more. Sorry, no. We're on the right page.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mrs. Mihajlovic, do you see there --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could reduce it just a tiny, bit, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The date is the 29th of September, the top of the page, and the first meeting scheduled and noted there is 1100 hours meeting with the municipal War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And again, if you could explain the full entry to the Chamber. It has a plus sign, so is it correct, according to your evidence, that the meeting occurred?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That means that the meeting was held and that it lasted until 2000 hours, as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could we have the previous page in English on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And so you just mentioned that it had 2000 hours. That is at the end of the entry; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Not -- up until 2000 hours. That's what it means. That was the first duty he had on that day, the first meeting, from 1100 to 2000 hours, to 8.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. And then I think we can see the rest of the meetings that occurred on that day are all after 2000 hours?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, again I tender --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could we ask Ms. Mihajlovic to read out the first two lines on the B/C/S page.

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Plus "1100 hours, meeting with the presidents of the War Presidency -- municipal War Presidencies." And the second one is a minus, and then there's a telephone number 332-611, Professor Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we see the minus sign in the English translation?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can go to the following page. Your Honour, that's a plus, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that's an error in translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's an error in translation, and it will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Can we go back to the first page. Where do we see not until 2000 hours?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At the end of the entry, Your Honour. Right down the bottom of the page in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I mean in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At the end -- at the end of the entry. You can see the word "Twenty." Twenty hundred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just beneath "1995."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Ms. Mihajlovic, is -- is -- from your reading of this entry, do you understand that the meeting commenced at 11.00 and finished at 2000 hours from your understanding of reading that entry now?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender that document 65 ter 0 -- sorry. 65 ter 13684 again for the limited purpose as discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, do you still maintain your objection for the purpose of admitting that 1st Krajina Corps document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I think that in this situation since it's probably a document that could be admitted from the bar table at least we can not object to its full admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It will be fully admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 4361.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That completes my examination-in-chief, Your Honour. If we could deal with the associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Except for those that were already admitted, are there any objections, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we take a look at 65 ter 21458, which is a log-book. What log-book is this, Ms. Mihajlovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a log-book where we recorded the documents that left the institution, documents that were assigned a certain number and that were registered in this book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you're tendering it in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That will be all admitted and given a new number in due course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And also, sorry, I forgot to mention, Your Honour, in the Rule 92 ter notification 10832 is actually already admitted as Exhibit P02820.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mrs. Mihajlovic, your statement was admitted in lieu of your oral testimony in this case, and then you will be further

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Ms. Mihajlovic.

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to thank you for having been so kind as to meet with me and my associate. I hope that this will help us finish this cross-examination quickly.

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: The pleasure was mine as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like us to go through a few things from your statement. I have to remind myself, actually, to pause between question and answer so that we do not exhaust our interpreters. In paragraph 23 -- actually, do you have your amalgamated statement printed out? Do you have it there?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could Mrs. Mihajlovic please be given a copy of her amalgamated statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You started working in the president's office in the beginning of 1993, regardless of who this president may be?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you have the transcript, you can see when the interpretation is over. I mean, I paused now waiting for the interpretation to finish. You are talking about the establishment of different services. That is what you refer to in this paragraph. And you also talk about advisors and associates. This is what I wanted to ask you: At that point in time, did I travel often, especially to Geneva, Belgrade, and elsewhere, and were all of these trips exclusively made for the purpose of negotiating for peace?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, you travelled often and for that purpose, and I think that that is recorded in our books, in our notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that the days when there was nothing were primarily Sundays, whereas on Saturdays I would come and work at the office?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I think that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that my advisors read reports from the field, everyone in their own particular areas, and they underlined what I should focus on, or they would tell me when we talked about what I should focus on since there were a great many reports?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In my absence, did the service function as follows: The advisors would receive reports, and if there was something urgent, they would address the ministries or the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 25 and further on, there is a description of the stay in Banja Luka. We saw the reports today. This period in Banja Luka, was it marked by the fall of many municipalities, and large parts of territory in western Bosnia -- or, rather, in western Republika Srpska, Croatia and NATO enter the war?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, yes, that was the main reason why you were there for a longer period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember a document in which Gordana Milinic asked for the reports to be sent to Banja Luka because for some time they were not being sent to Banja Luka, so we did not have insight into what was happening?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps we'll find it some other time. In paragraph 28, you say that there were lots of people, panic, chaos. Do you remember that from all of these municipalities that were falling then, namely Drvar, Glamoc, Grahovo, Bosanski Petrovac, Jajce, and later on Mrkonjic Grad as well, do you remember that all of these people who were refugees flooded Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I was there briefly. I came after you, but I know that the situation was chaotic in the streets of Banja Luka, that people were panic-stricken. It was a very bad picture. There was no electricity. It was totally chaotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that in the beginning of August hundreds of thousands -- actually, over 200.000 Serbs from Krajina, from the Serb Krajina, passed through Banja Luka as well as they were trying to reach Serbia as refugees after Croatian Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did that lead to an increase in fear, and was it reminiscent of the fall of the Serb Krajina, or was there fear that Republika Srpska would fall as well because these municipalities were falling one after the other?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the way it seemed. People were panic-stricken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 29, you say Professor Koljevic, Professor Plavsic, and Momcilo Krajisnik could see me without having made an appointment as high-ranking officials, eminent persons. Do you agree that nevertheless their visits would be recorded in your diary?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 36, you talk about how telephone calls were made, and you say -- I'm going to read it out in English: [In English] "If the president at that time received a telephone call, he could maybe speak on the phone for 30 minutes and that almost an hour does not mean that really somebody spoke with him for almost an hour." [Interpretation] I would like us to clarify something. For example, if you would write down that somebody entered my office at 1.00 in the afternoon and stayed until 6.00 in the afternoon, and in the meantime I would receive other persons as well, would that mean that they were all in the same room, or could I leave one room and receive other people while that first delegation would be working with somebody else?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. That kind of thing would happen. Would you receive some people in your office, and then some other people would come. You could leave and leave these people in your office so that you could receive some other people in some other room within your office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask you to take a look at the 14th of July, when there was a visit from the delegation of the municipality of Srebrenica, Skelani, headed by Mr. Deronjic. We are calling that up, but in the meantime can we have a look at the next page and paragraph 41. Forty-one refers to the period from April 14 through 16. It says that there is no information there. Do you remember that on the 15th of April, the 50th Assembly of Republika Srpska was held in Sanski Most, and is that the reason why your diary or log-book was empty?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: The log-book was certainly empty because you were not active in your office. I don't remember that the Assembly session was held at that point in time, but what is certain is that you were absent from the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think it's the log-book -- no. No. The log-book is not picture. No. Can somebody help us with the number, the number of this diary, the log-book, the secretary's diary?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: For 1995, it's Exhibit P02242.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have that in e-court and then the date of the 14th of July in that document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that Churkin, Ambassador Churkin, was scheduled for 1800 hours, but he arrived at 1925 hours, and stayed until 2240 hours?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that Miroslav Deronjic and the delegation of Srebrenica were scheduled for 11.00 and they arrived -- what time was this? 12.40.

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I think 14.25.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I see. 14.25 and they stayed until 18.25; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but there is this bit of information a bit further up, and I think that is unclear. It says 12.40 in parentheses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I see. Does it pertain to Ostojic and Karadzic, or you don't know?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me take a look. One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Just a second. We can -- for the purpose of -- yes. We zoom in for -- a bit further. Yes. So can you tell us what the -- the item which says 12.40 to 13.10 refers to what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember, but it could mean that Miroslav Deronjic was there only in that period. And later on, this other period of time, the delegation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that Karadzic and Ostojic were scheduled for that time for the following day and then they stayed for that period of time?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure, because there is a minus before that. They were certainly planned for that day, but they probably remained to be seen on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So the period for the delegation of Srebrenica and Deronjic, that is 14.25 to 18.25. Let us take a look further down and see who else came to see me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In -- in the meantime, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... wasn't what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime, I wanted to note that the minus for Professor Karadzic and Ostojic was not correctly reflected in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, no. I actually noted it myself and I was going to bring it to your attention that that is also something that we will have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So can you upload the English translation as well. So, in your view, the English translation on the right side is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is that a question to Mrs. Mihajlovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mrs. Mihajlovic. Mr. Deronjic stayed from 12.40 to 13.10, and together with the delegation from 14.25 to 18.25?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From 14.25 until 18.25. That's what this note should mean. However, the plus is a mistake. The plus further up. Professor Karadzic and Velibor Ostojic, there's a minus there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the marking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. About the 12.40 to 13.10, what does it refer to, Mrs. Mihajlovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since it's unclear and our notes are sort of squeezed in, it may relate to Mr. Deronjic, because it's right above his name, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, do you agree that in that same period of time, say beforehand from 13.45 until 18.25, Professor Koljevic and Ljubisa Vladusic were in one of the rooms there and that I also worked with them during that period of time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then Krajisnik, the speaker of the Assembly, was there from 10 past 2.00 until 4.15, so this same period of time. So I was sharing this time while these people were there. I was receiving him, too.

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then you can see that the others were also received -- let's just take a look at this. From 17.00 onwards, Bob Djurdjevic until 19.15. Actually from 17.00 to 19.15. Again this overlaps part of the time that the delegation from Srebrenica spent there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So while I was receiving other people, the delegation was working with other people -- or, rather, doing something else, while I was walking from one visitor to another; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We see here that Vladimir Dimitrijevic was there. Do you agree that this is an eminent publisher, the owner of L'Age d'Homme from Lausanne and Paris?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I remember his name and I know that he's a man from Paris, but I forgot the other details. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that it was easy to get to me and that I was happy to receive people, especially people who were from the diaspora and I had my picture taken with them and there were no restrictions whatsoever? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I do agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was tendered in its entirety?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to assist us in explaining how, at the time when you worked, documents were created, that is to say how they were received and processed. Am I correct in saying that a document produced after a meeting or an oral or written request by an institution was typed out either by you or Milijana? I signed it then, following which a copy would be kept for the archives and an original copy was sent to the addressee or to the encoding centre. Can you explain how a document was created and processed.

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: When a document was ready to be sent out, it means it had been typed out, signed by you or the chef de cabinet or one of the advisors. Next, the document was registered in the Protocol Book and assigned a specific number. Then it was sent to the addressee. If it was the Main Staff, usually the documents were sent through the communications centre. It also happened that if a document was for an institution which was at the same location as we, then it was taken by the courier. In any case, a copy was always kept in the cabinet and put in our binders in the archive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement you discuss that, but please assist us in clarifying the following: When we were in the same building with the Assembly, was there a period when there was a common Protocol Book and common archives? Does it mean that some documents from the beginning of the war were kept in the joint archives?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I recall, at the time when we were physically in the same building with the National Assembly, all joint administrative affairs were handled by the appropriate administrative office of the Assembly. It was Ms. Rajka Stanisic who was in charge of the archives, as well as Marina Ratkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that from the start the bureaucratic apparatus of the National Assembly was far larger in size than the presidential office's staff?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. The cabinet of the republican president at the time only employed a secretary and a chef de cabinet. All other general administrative affairs were handled by the appropriate office of the National Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you recall when we separated physically from the Assembly, when we went to the Famos managing building?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I know it was sometime in 1994, although I no longer recall the month. In any case, it all had to do with the arrival of Mr. Dmicic as chef de cabinet. Upon his arrival, he restructured the service of the president of the republic and expanded it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you learn at some point that Mr. Dmicic, who is a university professor nowadays, was Deputy General -- Secretary-General of the common Presidency before the elections in 1990 and we left him in that position following the 1990 elections, although he was not a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that he restructured the president's service as of 1994, later, based on his experience when the office of Secretary-General was established as well, so his position was no longer chef de cabinet?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: After the president's office service was formed, he became the Secretary-General and we moved to another location.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that all documents that the Presidency had or were sent from the president's office -- do you agree that all documents the Presidency had were sent from the president's office or received by the president's office?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was a document created that was not sent to someone else but just kept in the president's office, or were all documents either received or sent?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: They were all either received or sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In other words, if the presidential archives went missing, could such documents be found elsewhere, either as documents received by the Presidency and kept -- of which a copy was kept, or that they were sent from the president's office and that they kept the original?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your view, what size was the archive? How many binders or what size of truck one would need to transport it all.

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I remember that the archives were in large closets with many shelves and many binders. We really tried to register and archive each and every document. There were many binders, and I think you would need quite a large truck for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Although you were on maternity leave, do you remember, as you mentioned it in your amalgamated statement, that in the summer of 1998, you were warned by the --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'd like the cite for that in the witness's amalgamated statement, because I don't believe it is there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is possible. I have read everything else and perhaps it was omitted from the amalgamated statement by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But can the witness confirm, if indeed it is not in the amalgamated statement, whether something happened in the president's office in the summer of 1998 when you were advised not to enter the Presidency building?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I was not on maternity leave at the time. I was still pregnant. It was in August 1998. I went to work but was warned by the person who was on duty at the gate of the Famos factory that some people entered the presidential premises, and given the fact that I was pregnant, the man advised me that it would be better for me not to go to work and to go home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it not after the killing of the regional police chief at Pale, Srdjan Knezevic, who was a celebrated fighter? He was assassinated by terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I heard that late Mauzer's men were the ones who broke into the presidential premises, but I didn't go there, so I didn't see anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that after the split between Ms. Plavsic and the SDS, Mauzer was appointed to a senior police position and that as the head of investigating team, he came to Pale to investigate the murder of the late Knezevic?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that even witnesses were kept tied up there for a week, let alone those who were suspected of having done so? Was it not a terrible period of time where even witnesses suffered?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that some people were tied up there, and it is correct that -- that it was a very insecure, unsafe time. But I didn't go there. I didn't see it. I just know that everyone talked about it. It was a well-known fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: By that time, I no longer came to the office. I had stopped coming a few months before; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You were not there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in late 1996 and early 1997, that is to say in December and January, The Hague investigators visited Republika Srpska and Pale? On both occasions, they could access the entire archives and copied whatever they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I remember that. Did I not personally take part in the photocopy process, but I do know that some of my work colleagues were included in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you returned after a month or so to the office, what did you find?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean in 1998 when Mauzer was there?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was waiting for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was for about a month that we did not come to work. We returned later, and we no longer found the archives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, is it the -- is it the accused's position that on both occasions they could access -- that is, the OTP could access the entire archives and copied whatever they wanted, because we have had evidence to the contrary. Is that his position?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, by the entire archives, what did you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To my knowledge, they had access to everything that was otherwise not stipulated under the law as state secret. After the law on co-operation with this Tribunal was promulgated, they even had access to that because the state secret designation was removed from the documents. I also know that they seized over 300 documents at the time. It is also a fact that the first government to co-operate with this Tribunal was precisely the Government of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you satisfied with that answer, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's carry on. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the state of the premises? Was something else missing? Were the rooms empty?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I remember that the door to our office was locked. There were no signs of breaking and entry, but when we got inside, the cabinets where the archives were empty. I don't recall any other details. There was a mess. At least not in our office -- there was a mess in other offices but in ours, things seemed to be tidy save for the missing binders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Although the presidential archives were taken away, it seems, by someone, could the copies of all documents be found in other locations?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think so, because for the most part the documents were sent to us. So the sender should have kept their copies, or in other cases, we sent those documents to someone else and they should have their copy as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know of the existence of the international committee to find out the truth about Radovan Karadzic, which was founded in Belgrade, which is headed by Professor Smilja Avramov and Kosta Cavoski, who is the president, and other prominent professors and professionals from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard of that organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that they published six books of my wartime orders, wartime letters, interviews, and statements, as well as pardons? They published it in six volumes. They published all the documents that they could find.

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that the liaison person in Pale was my daughter Sonja? She communicated with the cabinet and people such as Mitar Kokolj and others who had some of our documents, so that the documents were gathered by her and then made part of the books? She did the work, not someone from the cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In any case, I didn't take part in that, so it could be Sonja, although I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At that time you were on maternity leave.

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I was on maternity leave twice, from January 1996 and again from January 1999. In both cases for a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we have a look at 1D5040. Thank you. Is this the first book from the series that contains a number of my wartime orders? And they printed my signature here. It's the sail signature on all the books?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's probably the book. If I could see the contents, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page now. Can we leaf through the preface so that we get to the other documents. So could we please move on from this page. Could we please leaf through the book. Can we move further. This is the preface written by Professor Cavoski. I think we have all of this in English too. So can we finally get to the documents now. Further on, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At that point in time you were not working, but the members of the Presidency were -- aha. This is already the 12th of May, so it's all three of us. This was the constituent session of the Presidency. Perhaps you don't know this but until the 12th of May, I was not on the Presidency but I was selected on the 12th of May. So can we move on to 1993. Can we just skip 1992 altogether.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I was going to say that Mr. Karadzic should refrain from his comment and put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic. What is your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would like us to move further on from this document, to 1993, and then I'm going to put a question. Yes, now we have a document. Can it be enlarged, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From December 1993. Is this what the documents looked like, those that were created in our office or cabinet? Could this please be enlarged. Do you recognise the form and also the number, the registration number? Can you explain this to the Trial Chamber, what it is that we see here?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise this. We see the letterhead of the president, and it says Republika Srpska, president of the republic, Sarajevo, underneath. That's in the right-hand corner. The left-hand corner shows the addressees, the Government of Republika Srpska, the GS, that is to say, the General Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, the MUP, the Ministry of Health, and the co-ordinating body of the government. Below is the number 01-400/93. That is the number from the log-book where we registered all the outgoing documents from the office and then the date when the document was created, that is the 18th of December, 1993. So that is something that reflects how we worked. If I can see the signature and seal then I can be more certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you something before we move on from this page. What does this mean 01, and what does 400 mean? Does it only pertain to that year?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: 01 is the number that we always placed before each document that left our institution; that is to say, every number would start with 01. And 400 is the number from the log-book, and 1993 means that it was registered in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. 01, who does that denote? If Dmicic or an advisor sent this document, would it also be 01?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as a rule it would have to denote you. So I'm not quite sure. I think that that is how we marked the documents signed by advisors as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If they wrote on my behalf; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Supposedly. That's the way it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we have the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the record, we are looking at e-court page 84. Yes. Please carry on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have a translation of the document on the right. The number is the same, 01-400/93. And on the left-hand side do you see whether this is the usual -- actually, can the left side be zoomed in. Yes, the Serbian version. Is this something that was quite customary, my title, signature, stamp? Can you explain this to the Trial Chamber? What is -- what is it that makes this document a presidential documents?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Primarily your signature and the stamp on that signature which is proof of the fact that that is your signature and that this document was created in our institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, is it time for the break now or should I go on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break for an hour and resume at 1.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.32 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could I just advise the Trial Chamber that in consultation with the Registry and the Defence, that we have arranged for the next witness not to be brought to the Tribunal in light of today's schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the Serbian version, the last page of this document. Does it look like what you would otherwise expect from such a document in terms of language and format?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is what I would expect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So it says "Protocol 01-400/93." It means the 400th document in that year. So every year began with 01-1 -- or 01.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we keep leafing through the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I thought that the witness said before the break that the 01 stood for the president, not for the first document of the year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But she referred to the next numbers after 01-.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. In Mr. Karadzic's question he says so every year began with 01, but I --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I understood the 01 in protocol 01-400/93. I understood the 01 in that context was to mean it was sent from the president and it was document number 400. That was my understanding of her evidence before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Having heard your intervention, I take it Mrs. Mihajlovic can explain that in clearer terms.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first two digits, 01, means that the document was created in the president's office. -400 means it is the document number in the Protocol Book. That is document number 400 for that year. Once we were in the next year, the first document produced was marked as 01-01. The second 01 is the ordinal number in the Protocol Book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now is it clear, Ms. Sutherland? I think that's what witness said.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What do you have to tell us about this document then in terms of numbers? It seems to be the beginning of 1994, and it seems that already on the 1st of January, eight documents were produced; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we go to the next original. You can keep leafing through. Can we go -- yes. Orders. Yes. Can we go one by one, the original documents. Please zoom in. Not in the English language, the Serbian, please. Is this the 281st document that year, and it was only the 7th of February, 1994. Also, is the format something that you would expect it to be?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Keep going, please. Just the originals, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, can we show Ms. Mihajlovic the whole set of books so that she can identify them?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this from May? It seems that on the 19th of May, there were already 955 documents; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have a stamp. The protocol number seems to be correct. It was signed; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, could we ask Ms. Mihajlovic to go through the books? These are collections of documents created by the president's -- created by the president's office and certified by either this witness or her colleague, and the documents were sent to different addressees. They conclude [as interpreted] wartime letters, wartime orders, et cetera. It's all in e-court, but perhaps it would be easier for the witness to peruse it as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, do you object to the admitting of this compilation or book?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If Your Honour can give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I understood at the moment the issue of admission is not on the table. It's more a question of the format in which the witness reviews at least certain portions of that documentation. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But that was asked in order to tender it into evidence. So I wanted to pre-empt it. If there's no objection, there's no need to go through that procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime, do you have it in hard copy?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are all in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By the way, in e-court I have only 182 pages.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were scanned two-sided. All six books were scanned and uploaded in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does it contain all pages of those six books?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime, why don't we hand them over to the witness so then she can take a look. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, this isn't a complete collection. It's a selective collection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that was my point that I asked Mr. Karadzic, but he said to the contrary.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't take part in that. I was already up in the mountains when my colleagues published this, whatever documents could be sent to them by my daughter. It's definitely not all of the documents, but we have the majority of wartime letters and a fair amount of orders. I just wanted the witness to confirm that all these documents were created in our office. Many of them have already been admitted as individual documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please be precise in answering the question by the Chamber. I specifically asked you whether it contains all pages of those six books. Your answer was "Yes, absolutely," and now you're speaking otherwise. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think that what's in e-court does contain all of the pages of those books, but what he was trying to tell you is that what's in those books are not all of his orders and wartime letters, but everything that's in the book is in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In this number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe there's several numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I was advised just one book has only one 65 ter number. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But what's the point Mr. Karadzic is trying to make if this is only a selective version of the documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This being what --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is only a selective amount of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This being the book, the original book.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, but they don't contain every -- every order or decision that has ever been issued by him, and so what's the point of -- of submitting this selective few?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you -- is it your case that the entire -- compilation of entire order or documents exist?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are documents that have been issued by the president which are not included in these -- in these volumes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. So you're object to go the admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, I'm wondering what -- what the point Mr. Karadzic is trying to make with the witness with these documents, by tendering these selective number of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: But are you saying they're inadmissible? Are you saying that they're inadmissible?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, I'm not saying that, Your Honour. I'm simply saying that he's -- what is he trying -- what's the point that he's trying to make with the witness with these volumes of documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Well, he would know, presumably.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But if -- he's wanting the witness to say -- he's asked the witness: Are these all the documents that I produced? Well, unless the witness sits there for a day and goes through every page of every volume, she's not going to be able to confirm or deny. And even then, she may not be in a position, once she's reviewed them all, to answer that question he's put to her.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I intervene in language? I did not pretend [sic] to say: Are those all the documents produced in our cabinet? My question was: Are all of those documents produced in our cabinet?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Again, unless the witness is given a substantial amount of time to go through the volumes, she's not going to be able to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We heard the submission. Ms. Mihajlovic, do you have any observation after having looked at those six books?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I, before that, make a suggestion? We don't have to read it all. She was just asked to look at the protocol number and the stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think she testified and gave evidence as to how the book was compiled and published. Would you like to add anything, Ms. Mihajlovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I said was that I knew that such books were published and that some of my colleagues directly participated in their production. I did not, however, but I am aware of their existence. I leafed through book number 1 called "Wartime orders." I skipped the first part because it concerns 1992, when I was not employed by the president's office. However, as I keep going through 1993, I managed to view a few documents, and I can confirm that they were positively created in our office, and the layout is what we used in our work. Perhaps we should choose at random. I only managed to see only a small part of the first book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I noted that you wanted to say something, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't know if I can add any clarity to this discussion or not, Mr. President, but it does occur to me that the discussion thus far has not clearly identified both aspects of the admissibility issue or at least discussed them independently. One, of course, is the question of authenticity. Are those documents created under certain conditions, and then are they what they purport to be? And the second one is relevance. There are many documents which we can deem authentic under -- for various reasons under various circumstances and then the question is: Do they rise to the level which would justify admission in -- in this Chamber. And I think that's the issue upon which Ms. Sutherland was focusing before. We have no reason at this moment to challenge the authenticity of any of these documents in particular at this moment, but the relevance of such a volume of documents is something that might occur to us, particularly when the Prosecution has attempted on other occasions to get in other statements by the accused for reasons that we'd be happy to -- and have articulated at the time are relevant, but those have been deferred for subsequent bar table submission. So I don't want to make it more complicated, but I thought I wanted to bring us back to some of the factors that I thought had guided the admissibility process throughout.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you be a bit more specific as to what you had in mind by -- when you referred to the other accused's statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Speeches on video, interviews with newspapers. In my -- I mean, in those in -- in the system -- the domestic system from Mr. Robinson and I come, I think would be clearly admissible when made by an accused, and the question is not one of their authenticity. They're often on tape. Those, in many cases, have been deferred for bar table submission. Maybe that's not the most efficient way. Maybe they should just be let in as we proceed, but I think in an effort to abide by the standards that have -- we have been following as we progress, that was the nature of the reference that was made, and I think part of the reason why this volume of material was -- one of the comments about this volume of material were made at this time. So not so much the authenticity issue, which presumably this witness can illuminate to some extent, but the relevance issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. The Chamber will consider the issue and give its ruling in due course. In the meantime, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before that, can I -- can the Chamber be informed of the 65 ter numbers of those six volumes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. 1D5040, 5041, 5042, 5043, 5044, 5045 inclusive. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It includes not only the letters but also the interviews and speeches.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One of the books contains public appearances, speeches, et cetera. The other one deals with various charitable action -- actions. One contains letters to various heads of state and government, and the first book contains orders, wartime orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, just with respect to your last observation in relation to 65 ter number Defence 1D05045 containing the interviews and speeches, the Defence can't have it both ways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not only that, the previous version also has these similar contents, interviews and speeches.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I mean, this witness can't speak to the -- to the truth of the contents of them, but they want them in for -- for all purposes, and I would submit, for example, the interview with the Spanish journalist earlier today, "El Pais," which was admitted for the limited purpose which I sought to -- to tender it, we do have the audio. It is a recording of the accused, and that could be also admitted in its entirety given that it's an interview with the accused.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I thought at first the books contained only orders. We didn't know about the letters, interviews or speeches. Whatever the result may be, if you are to tender these documents -- books through this witness, you better deal with it one by one with this -- with this witness, in particular the letters and interviews and speeches, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry, the Prosecution wouldn't object if -- if the documents that we have sought to -- to tender for the limited purpose also came in for all purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I do not follow. Are you referring to that specific interview or as a whole about this book?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm saying that the Prosecution wouldn't object --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: To what?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: To Mr. Karadzic's speeches being tendered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- if -- if the -- any interviews that Mr. Karadzic gives that the Prosecution wishes to put in come in for all purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. You heard the intervention -- submission of Ms. Sutherland --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] I'm talking specifically about the two I used this morning with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not clear. If those two are to be admitting, you are not objecting to the admitting of those last two volumes? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm just saying that Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Robinson objected this morning when I initially sought to tendere the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I see your point.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And I clarified how I was seeking to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, your point is taken. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In relation to this, I'd like to say the following: The letters and orders are documents that I can stand by.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the interviews, I have not authorised them. That's the difference. I have not authenticated the interviews, and, for instance, made objections or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're not giving evidence, and what I told you, we heard some foundation about the first volume which contains your orders during the wartime. You didn't lead any evidence in relation to other volumes. In order to tender them, what I said is to lead -- ask questions, ask questions to this witness. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ms. Mihajlovic, would you please take a look -- after you've looked at the orders, could you take a look at the book containing letters. Are those letters also -- do they appear to be authentic, and if you look at the form, have they also been produced and drafted at the office -- by the office of the president?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Should we upload 65 ter 5041.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm leafing through this book, and what I can observe is that these letters do not bear signatures or stamps on the basis of which I could confirm that they were indeed produced by the office of the president, but what I do recall with certainty is that you did send letter to many of these individuals. I cannot recall the content, obviously, but I do know that you exchanged or wrote to these individuals quite frequently.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the next page in e-court so that we can take a look at one of the sample letters. This is just the introduction. Can we move on? These are not letters. Could we, for instance, take a look at page 20, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, here, these are not facsimile. This is retyped?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I can see that your signature's missing as well as the stamp, but I do recall with certainty that you wrote letters to these individuals very frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, if there is any problem with these letters, can I just say that they were within my control, whereas the interviews weren't, so if I hadn't authenticated them, that's how it is. But the letters I can authenticate, because they were under my control. And if this is acceptable, the Trial Chamber could benefit from obtaining -- looking at these letters that refer to various situations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably the Chamber would be benefitted if it hears from you, Mr. Robinson, as to this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, I advised Dr. Karadzic to move on and use his time with this witness on other things, because I think it's not possible to admit these globally at this point. We can do that through other means, but given that this is an important witness and there's other important things to cover, I think it's better for him to seek to admit these documents with -- through another means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you are not tendering those six volumes in its entirety, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think it would be difficult to tender all of those six volumes given the fact that they contain a variety of items, including interviews. So I think it's better for us to be more selective and tender them at a time when we can do that and not lose some opportunities to obtain important information from the current witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's proceed. I thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we then have 1D5040 one more time so that you may identify several other documents, and then I will move on to a new topic. Could we please move towards the end of the book. Towards the end. This is still 1992. Very well. Here we are. Could we now see the document that I have requested. That's on the next page, please. Is this a standard document produced in November 1995, which means that the preceding document would have been 2053?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this one is 2054.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It's 2054. Now, could you tell us, please, what kind of stamp is this that we see on the top of the page?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if we can just zoom in on that part only, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is the handwriting that we see there? What does that mean, and what is the significance of this? It says "Delivered --"

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, now I recall. This means that this document was sent to the Main Staff of VRS via the communications centre. It means that somebody took this document to the communications centre and it is probably there that this document was stamped in this manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And it was received there at 19.20, and it was then delivered at 20.45.

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They received it at 19.20, and they forwarded it onward at 20.40.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we see the next page, please. This is after the signing of the Dayton Accords. It's one of the orders. The content is irrelevant, just the format. Let's take a look at the form of this letter. This, too, is a standard form, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would request P -- or, rather, 1D2739. Please take a look at this document. Was this document produced at our office? This is not an order. Rather, it is decision on -- a decision on a pardon. I don't think this document has been admitted, or has it? Is this a decision on pardoning the individuals mentioned below?
