If you look at the names, would you agree that all of these individuals were -- are Muslims, and it says they're from Prijedor and Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The names are Muslim names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was this drafted in our office? In the preamble it says, "Pursuant to the constitution and the legal basis," and so on, and then it's a decision. Was this produced at our office?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, very frequently when the document in question was a decision, then the date would be at the bottom of the page. That was the form. But I believe that this document was -- as we can see in Article 2, it was published in the Official Gazette of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does the number at the bottom of the page refer to the fact that it was produced by the president's office, number 01-562?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well, this will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 4362.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please keep on the left-hand side the Serbian version. And now I would like to call up 5039. And can we just keep on the screen the Serbian version, please? 1D2739. I'm sorry, P3039. It's Prosecution Exhibit P3039. Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you please take a look at the heading and protocol. What can you tell us about this when you compare them to the documents produced at the office the president?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: This document was not produced at the cabinet -- at the office of the president. I'm sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a document from the end of 1993, and then we see that for the entire year the number is 02 -- 2 and then -934; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, but this is not our document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have the next page, please. The Serbian version, the last page. Could you please read out who drafted this document, who typed it up, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is -- the page we are seeing on left side is a different one, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. On the left-hand side we are showing the form of a document sent from the office of the president, and now we would like to show what a document that wasn't produced at the office of the president looks like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document was definitely not produced at the office of the president of the republic. It is obvious due to several reasons. First of all, your position, the supreme commander. We never signed your name that way. Also, the note that says that it was typewritten in a single copy. That's strange, because I've already said, we always had several copies. One was went to the addressee and another stayed in the archives. So there was never a single copy only. Thirdly, the full stop after DR. And also the fact that the document was typewritten in the Roman script. We always did our typing in Cyrillic. That is something that I noticed, and that is why I believe this document was definitely not created in the office of the republic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Because of the overlapping, the interpreters couldn't hear you. Would you repeat your question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the elements that indicate creation were not created in the office, but somebody brought this and got the signature he wanted and the stamp.

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is your signature and stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, there is no copy in the Presidency, because they did not -- it was in a single copy.

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpret did not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat what you just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: P838. It's a Prosecution exhibit, 838. Thank you. Please take a look at the letterhead here as well, the protocol involved, and everything that has to do with the creation and the origin of the document.

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Could this be enlarged, please? This document was not created in the president's office either. The letterhead is not right, and the number of the register is not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is directive for further operations number 7 that is rather well known in this trial and in this courtroom. Can we have the last page now. Could the lower part please be zoomed in so the witness can see it properly. What is your conclusion on the basis of the end of this document?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yet again, this is not the office that we put on the documents that we generated. And number two, the stamp is not the stamp of the president of the republic but, rather, of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we zoom in on the stamp, because in the translation there is no reference to the contents. And could you please read out what it says on the stamp?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: It says the "Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In this documents, it's not only that it wasn't created in the Presidency, but it wasn't even brought to the Presidency for signing and stamping.

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: We may conclude that because it bears the stamp of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So much for directives 6 and 7. Now I'd like to ask for 1D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Mihajlovic, how about the signature? Is it Mr. Karadzic's?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I could say with certainty that it is his signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we take a look at the top of the page. How many pages are there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland. Was it because of that that you rose?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that the pages are not numbered. Can someone help us with the number of pages that this document has?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's about 24, but probably including the cover letter or -- it's 21 pages, if I'm correct. Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we see the penultimate page in Serbian, we'll be able to tell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 20 or -- or page 19. There are blank pages every other page. Its format is very strange. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a matter of re-scanning, if it's done from back to front.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there are 10 or 11 pages. Eleven pages, can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Eleven pages in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In view of the time that you spent in the office and the fact that you're familiar with my habits, would you agree that I signed shorter documents without reading them, let alone a long document like this if the documents were prepared by one of my collaborators?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the assumption that this is really my signature, that it was signed, rather, would you agree that it had to be signed somewhere else, not in the office or cabinet itself, because there would have been a stamp had it been signed in the office?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: That is certainly the way it would have been done had it been done at the office of the president of the republic. It would have borne the stamp of the president the republic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, can Mr. Karadzic put his case in relation to this document? Did he sign -- he has said -- he's put it to this witness that he didn't sign this document. Is that his case, that he didn't sign directive 7?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't think that Dr. Karadzic has put his case to this witness in that way, but it's not -- when and if he gives evidence, he can give that answer, but it's his case. It's simply to elicit from the witness the nature of the document, including the signature, the stamps, and the other things. So he's not required to give in the middle of the trial his evidence or his position as to a particular piece of evidence. You've heard the answers from the witness, and we'll each be able to argue what you should conclude from that at the end of the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, under Rule 90(H) he has to put his case. This is a matter that's disputed between the parties, and he has to put his case to the witness. The witness has said that it's his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: And he's not seeking to impeach the witness on that answer at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, you referred to the impeachment of the -- or cross-examination, but here how do you read Rule 90(H)(ii): "In the cross-examination of a witness who is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examining party, counsel shall put to that witness the nature of the case of the party for whom that counsel appears, which is in contradiction of the evidence given by the witness"? So your case is that she never gave contradictory evidence so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And it is not now that he should give his case at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, would you like to respond?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The witness was asked by Your Honour how about the signature, "Is it Mr. Karadzic's?" And she said, "Yes, I can say with certainty that it is his signature." Now, if it's Mr. Karadzic's case that it's not his signature, then he has to put it to her that it's not his signature and he didn't sign it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was he not asking where it was possibly signed?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. He says: "Q. In this document, and it's not only that it wasn't created in the Presidency, but it wasn't even brought to the Presidency for signing and stamping."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, but you said on the assumption that this is really my signature. Rather, would you agree that it had to be signed somewhere else, not in the office of the cabinet itself. Because that was asked after having heard from the witness that it was your signature. Then I think, to that extent, Ms. Sutherland has a point. If you have to challenge that it was not your signature then you have to put your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: If we were challenging that it was not his signature, then we would put our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So it is your case that it is not Mr. Karadzic's signature?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, that's not our case, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not your case. I misunderstood. Thank you. That clarifies everything. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe all this confusion was created by the interjected phrase, the phrase that I interjected. Even if I did sign this elsewhere, we can disregard all of that together. My question to the witness is as follows:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was this signed at the cabinet? The directive number 6 was probably signed at the cabinet and has the stamp of the office of the Presidency. So that's the only difference between directives 6 and 7, where it was signed, but both documents were created elsewhere. Would you agree with that, Witness?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree that this document was not signed in the cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to ask for 1D5037. Can you tell us now what the difference is between these two certifications?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: The first difference is in the name of the office you hold. We would usually write down the office that is on the left-hand side, that is to say, "President of the republic and the supreme commander of the Army of Republika Srpska." However, we did not always add "supreme commander." We always put "president of the republic," but sometimes we also did say "and supreme commander of the Army of Republika Srpska." On the right-hand side is "The office of supreme commander." We certainly did not do this at our office. That is not the way that we would refer to the office you held. That is not the office that you held that we placed above your signature. Also, there's a difference involving the stamp. On the left-hand side is the president of the republic, and on the right-hand side is the stamp of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you need to tell us the origin of these stamps. Where did you collect them?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Yes, Ms. Sutherland, was that your point?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it the right one is from directive 7, and the left one comes from where, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Any document. It's from any document. It's typical. But if it's of assistance, 1D5036. Can we call that up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mrs. Mihajlovic, that in the corner on the left there is the letterhead and the end of directive number 6, and on the right-hand side the same, the end of number -- directive number 7 and that all the other stamps are from any document that was created in our office?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Could it be enlarged a bit more, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you zoom in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here where it says directive 6 and directive 7, those are not our log-book numbers; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I was going to say. Neither the heading where it says "Supreme Command of the armed forces of Republika Srpska," nor the protocol number are ours. They certainly were not produced at the office of the Presidency. And then the signature and the title, as I've already said, the supreme commander is not the title that we usually used at the office of the president when we put your name as the undersigned of a document, and also the stamp is not -- it's a stamp from the Main Staff. It's not from our cabinet. And I think in a document which says directive 6, there is a dot after doctor, and it's also in the Latin script which definitely means that it wasn't at the -- it wasn't produced at the office of the president. And also after Dr, doctor, we do not put a dot. That's not proper in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, it is proper if you're half literate, correct, semi-literate? Now, the two that were not produce by the Presidency, what do they refer to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness cannot answer that question from the document that she's got in front of her. Mr. Karadzic took her earlier to directive 6 and directive 7 separately. And if he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But in the previous document 1D5037, the witness said that the left stamp and the format were consistent with other -- Mr. Karadzic's signature at the time, didn't she?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So on that basis we have a basis to admit that document, don't we?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, these -- these are simply cutting and pasting from the top of the documents and the bottom of the documents, and are identified as directive 6 and directive 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For convenience of comparison, I'm referring to the previous document, 1D5037. Do you object to admitting this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, but -- but what I'm saying is the witness has been taken to the full documents of directive 6 and directive 7 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- and, rather, those are admitted documents rather than admitting this piece of paper which purports to be the stamps from those two documents. You actually have those two documents that you can look at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Those -- directive 6 and directive 7 were already admitted, weren't they? Those two have P number already.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will get Mr. Reid to give them to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, they were admitted, yes. And then this 1D5037 will be a convenient tool to compare the signature part. So on that basis we can admit this. Yes, this will be admitted as the next Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D2057, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, carry on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, in view of the charges and the indictment where it is claimed that we were intolerant of other ethnicity as well as that we were insensitive to the suffering of civilians, wherever they were -- they came from, including our own, I would like to ask you this: What was the position, not only my personal position but also our entire office as well as the entire official part of Republika Srpska, what was our position and our attitude towards Muslims and Croats, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, and I can only speak about myself and about you, as far as I know, you were not in any way intolerant of other ethnicities. You never displayed any such position. I, at least, never witnessed that. On the contrary, I am aware of the fact that among the closest of your associates, including your counsellors, there were people of other ethnicities or people who came from mixed marriages or who were -- or who were themselves in mixed marriages. In other words, married to people of other ethnicities. So one could absolutely not say that you were intolerant of other ethnicities. As for others, I really couldn't speak about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But do you agree with me that a Catholic church remained standing in downtown Pale, that my hairdresser was a Croatian woman, that there was no -- not a trace of intolerance in respect of those people?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's correct. The Catholic church remains at Pale to this day. I live there. And I do recall your hairdresser, and I know that she was a Croatian and I know because we frequently made reference to that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You probably had occasion to see and type up a lot of documents produced or sent on my behalf where I intervened on the matter of humanitarian aid and humanitarian issues. Do you recall that the vice-president -- Vice-president Koljevic, who was a very respectable man, the second person in the republic was actually appointed to the post of commissioner for humanitarian matters?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree it was necessary for me to strengthen this role of his and that I sent orders to the effect that humanitarian convoys should be allowed through and similar? And do you recall that there were a lot of documents to that affect that were sent out from the office because there were many humanitarian convoys that were -- for some reason that were stopped or it was difficult for them to move on?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I do recall now that I saw a document just a moment ago, and there was your signature at the end of it, and I recall that you frequently intervened, and you frequently called on people to be careful and abide by the Geneva Conventions and the -- and to be careful about how they treated prisoners, and I know that you frequently intervened, and I know that sometimes you would get really upset about those instances where there were violations of your orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you agree with me that this was too much for me, for my office, so I nominated for this high position the vice-president, Mr. Koljevic, and as you recall, I was really very busy with work day and night, almost like 24-hour stores?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I remember that, and we can see that from the times indicated at the -- at some of those documents we saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you remember that mention was made when the Srebrenica was issue was discussed? Well, I won't ask you about 1993. Let me ask you about 1995. Did you ever hear or learn about the developments in Srebrenica -- or, rather, when was the first time that you heard of these developments?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, I heard about this incident from the media, and I am absolutely certain that I did not discuss this either with you or any other of your aides, and at first, to be honest, I didn't really believe what was reported in the media because the media frequently misrepresented or broadcast incorrect information but that's how I heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was the position at the office of the president that this was not -- actually, was the situation in the president's office such that this was not really discussed or at least wasn't a topic of discussion for a long time?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can recall, we did not discuss this. Well, especially I recall this because at the time I was pregnant and I was really quite absorbed by other things. I was focused on other matters, so I didn't really pay attention to information that I at the time considered incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I just ask you something about the amalgamated statement where you were asked about me, what kind of person I was, whether I had a tendency to yell at people. I don't know if it was in this statement or in the amalgamated statement, but would you tell the Trial Chamber what you know about me, not only what your opinion is about me but also the things that you know about me being a -- an educated, an intellectual person. So tell the Trial Chamber who was I. What kind of person was I as a president, as a human being, and a boss?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I can say that our relationship was purely professional. You were very kind and very respectful with all your assistants, not only your assistants but also all employees, including the lowliest, or, including the cleaning ladies and the waiters and so on. And I can say that everyone there respected you. You were not a person given to yelling. Perhaps there were times when you angry if people failed to carry out their duties, but I know for sure that you never raised your voice to me. What else can I say? Well, I think you were very dedicated to your family, which was something that really appealed to me. And I don't know if this is sufficient, and quite certainly my opinion is very positive, and I believe that it's a great pleasure -- I believe it would be a great pleasure for anyone to have that kind of boss. You were a very good boss. And as the president, you were not a person who tried to impose your authority, rather, you tried to lead and be -- work with your employees in a democratic way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That is very flattering. Thank you very much for your effort and for coming here to testify. I would like to wish you a pleasant stay here and a safe trip home, and, please, all the best to your family and your two daughter who were born once I fled into the hills.

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: And thank you very much, and all the best to you too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that the witness leave the courtroom for a short time. I wish to make a submission to you in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Mihajlovic, if you could excuse yourself for a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the Chamber move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We are now in open session, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I will need to call up a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I will need to call up another document first, and that is Defence Exhibit D01935.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Could we see the original of previous document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll come to that. So we'll deal with this exhibit first, 1935.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Ms. Mihajlovic, during your cross-examination, you -- Mr. Karadzic put to you that -- that when the OTP --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you hear me now, Ms. Mihajlovic? Now you do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's all right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please repeat, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I'm just finding ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mrs. Mihajlovic, earlier in cross-examination, Mr. Karadzic put to you that all of the archives were made available to the Office of the Prosecutor when they came to inspect the archives. Do you recall that? We are talking about in -- in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I remember that I know that, but I said that I was not directly involved in this work. This was done by my colleagues. Well, all the archives were there, but I don't know what they copied and what they took out. However, I know that they did work, that they did co-operate, that they did copy certain documents from the archives.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And we can see the document in front, which is D1935. This is an internal memorandum of -- of a mission to the area, and it's dated the 24th of February, 1998, about the mission earlier in the month. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And it was for the purpose of inspecting the records and the archives. I'd now like to read you a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if I could have the next document on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mrs. Mihajlovic, this is dated the 5th of February, 1998, so earlier in the month of the visit by the OTP investigators, and it's addressed to "Respected Mr. President," and it's from Milos Vukasinovic. This document is in English, so I will read the document to you: "I'm enclosing one of the singled-out documents which original copy was found in your archive. If an investigator finds this document, it would invalidate/revoke all documents in your defence. I will not explain in this letter its importance, because you will understand it as soon as you read it. However, you do not need to worry about today, because we inspected and prepared everything. This letter is a supplement to the previous lever which was not yet sent. I know you will destroy letters and document as soon as you are informed, but I still need to remind you to do right away?" Now, does -- does this letter make it clear to you that not all documents were made available to the -- to the Office of the Prosecutor when they inspected the archives?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would prefer not talking about this period, because as I said, I was not involved. I don't know exactly what was done. I know that the colleague who signed this, Milos Vukasinovic, and also there was Aleksandar Jovicevic, but, believe me, I would rather not answer that question because it would merely involve guesswork.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you have an opinion about -- about it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I think the witness has just given her opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that that is the way it is, and I would like to leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, could I tender this document, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What did you mean, Ms. Mihajlovic, when you said you thought that that was the way it was? Could you be a bit more specific?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you know what? If I were to give a comment or give an opinion, that would not be something that I know, rather, something that I think, and I would like to speak about things I know here. I believe that it would be guesswork if I were to comment upon a document that I'm not familiar with, and I don't even know if it was signed, and even if it were signed, I don't know if I would recognise Mr. Vukasinovic's signature, so it's better for me not to comment upon this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have no objection to the admission of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4370. Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mrs. Mihajlovic, what I was referring to when I asked if you had an opinion on this was that you earlier in your cross-examination proffered an opinion about all of the archives being made available to the Office of the Prosecutor, and I wonder now having reading this document whether you still stand by what you said earlier?

utterances.speaker: MIRA MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I think that all of the documents had been proffered because all the documents were where they were otherwise, and all these people probably could have had access to all of these documents. However, I cannot claim something that I don't really know about.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Milovanovic. That concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll rise all together. Tomorrow we resume at 9.00. The hearing is now adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 9th day of February, 2012, at 9.00 a.m.
